title: How a voice agent answers in about 600 ms
subtitle: Speech flows through turn detection, speech to text, an LLM and text to speech inside one tight latency budget.
hook: Callers notice past 500 ms, and turn detection listens to intonation, not just silence.

sources.title: Engineering voice agents: Latency, quality, and scale
sources.speaker: Rishabh Bhargava

sources.title: How to Build Voice Agents That Don't Fall Apart When You Interrupt
sources.speaker: Jesse Hall

nodes.label: Caller
nodes.detail: A real person on the phone, often on speakerphone in traffic with kids in the back seat, not clean benchmark audio.
nodes.tradeoff: People answer each other in about 300 ms; once an agent takes more than 500 ms, callers notice.

nodes.label: Agent orchestrator
nodes.detail: Receives the caller's streamed audio chunks and wires speech to text, the LLM and text to speech together. Pipecat and LiveKit are common choices.
nodes.tradeoff: In a pipeline, handling interruptions and barge-ins takes a lot more engineering than in a speech-to-speech model.

nodes.label: Speech to text
nodes.detail: Turns streamed audio into text; the best models get about 6% of words wrong on open benchmarks. A misheard name carries through every later step.
nodes.tradeoff: Whisper was trained on 30-second clips; newer streaming models look ahead only 80 ms to 1 second.

nodes.label: Turn detector
nodes.detail: Decides whether a pause means the caller has finished. LiveKit's model listens to rhythm, pitch and intonation, not only the transcript.
nodes.tradeoff: A leading alternative cut callers off 9.9% of the time; LiveKit's cut them off 4.5% on its hotel agent.

nodes.label: LLM
nodes.detail: Reads the transcript, decides whether to call a tool, and streams a reply. Text to speech needs a whole sentence, so time to first sentence matters.
nodes.tradeoff: About 300 ms to first token is the target, which points to 8B to 30B models; bigger burns the budget.

nodes.label: Async tools
nodes.detail: Looks up transactions, checks payment status or files disputes. Awaiting the call separately lets the conversation keep going meanwhile.
nodes.tradeoff: Some back-end calls take tens of seconds; that can't be hidden, so the agent keeps talking like a human would.

nodes.label: Text to speech
nodes.detail: Turns each sentence into audio chunks streamed back to the caller, ideally with the right accent, pronunciation and emotion.
nodes.tradeoff: The 200 ms here is the top of the 100 to 200 ms time to first audio the talk gives for a whole optimized setup, not a TTS-only figure.

nodes.label: Co-located inference
nodes.detail: Runs the models in the same data center as the orchestrator scales up early, and scales down only once live calls have finished.
nodes.tradeoff: Cutting network hops from 75 ms to 5 ms made an already tuned agent about 30% faster.

flow.text: Caller says they want to pay on the 3rd, then pauses.
Streams the caller's audio chunks to speech to text.
Finishes the transcript about 100 ms after the caller stops talking.
Hears the falling intonation and decides the caller's turn has ended.
Streams a reply and fires the payment tool without waiting on it.
Schedules the payment in the background while the conversation continues.
Speaks the first full sentence as soon as the LLM finishes it.
Hears the reply; a gap near 600 ms feels human.

takeaways.text: People reply in about 300 ms; past 500 ms callers notice, and at one to two seconds they hang up.
Hearing intonation, not just pauses, keeps the agent from cutting off a caller who says 'five hundred...' mid-amount.
Pick the stack by running simulated callers through whole conversations; leaderboards score single models on clean audio.
